Three different types of business analytics (in Excel)

Last week was pivot tables. This week stays on the left with charts.

Descriptive This week’s focus

Analyzes historical data to understand past business performance (e.g., describe sales from last three years).

Excel tools (examples)

    Predictive

    Uses (statistical) techniques to forecast future outcomes (e.g., predict next year’s sales based on historical data).

    Excel tools (examples)

      Prescriptive

      Recommends actions to optimize business outcomes (e.g., find the profit-maximizing price for a new product).

        Excel Charting

        Best practices for visualization

        Keep it simple

        • Focus on the key message.

        Know your audience

        • A CEO may need a different visual than the technical teams.

        Label charts well

        • Axis, legend, title.
        • But delete legends with one data series (no additional information).

        Remove noise

        • From your chart background (e.g., gridlines).

        Clean up your axes

        • – Avoid cluttered axes
        • – Remove unnecessary decimal places
        • – Avoid misleading colors (e.g., red may imply negativity)

        INSY 2299 · Session 7
        Excel Charting

        Different charts should be used for different purposes

        Pie charts

        Show pieces of a whole—that is, each slice of the pie shows how big one component of the whole is.

        So, pie charts are only meaningful if all the slices are positive and together all the slices add up to something meaningful (e.g., comparison of different expense-types).

        Pie charts should never be used to plot time-series data.

        Column charts

        Compare differences in groups (e.g., expense-types over time).

        Line charts

        Show trends over time (e.g., net income over several years).

        Mini Lab Exercise

        Mini lab exercise

        → Open the Visualization file:

        1. Navigate to the Ram Retail Planning Model sheet and create a Line Chart showing the trend of “Sales Revenue”, “Gross Profit”, “Earnings before Taxes” and “Net Income” over four years (2025–2028). Put the years on the X-axis (horizontal). Be sure to label the chart well and to include a legend.
        2. Navigate to the Stocks sheet and create a Scatter (X,Y) Chart to examine the relationship between “ADBE” (Series X Values) and “ORCL” (Series Y Values). Hint: Create an empty Scatter Chart and then in the “Select Data” dialog box, add the appropriate data series. Name the series “Correlation Stocks”.

        SELECTION

        INSY 2299 · Session 7
        Excel Roundup

        Data description: six criteria, 19 metro areas

        (1) Business Environment, (2) Human Capital, (3) Costs, (4) Quality of Life, (5) Transportation, (6) Geography. Geography is a bit more subjective than the other criteria, which are backed by “hard” data. Click a column header to sort; the leader gets a maroon outline.

        Data source: Moody Analytics; note that we included Seattle as reference point (italic)

        INSY 2299 · Session 7
        Excel Roundup

        Ranking category details

        Business environment

        State incentives, metro credit rating, state credit rating, 5/10 yr. job/tech job growth, tax environment

        Human capital

        New degrees in engineering, computers, math, new BA degrees, total pop degrees, supply/demand ratio

        Cost

        Single-family house prices, salary (biz/fin, mgmt, comp/math), costs of doing business

        Quality of life

        Crime rate, arts/entertainment/recreation & restaurants per 1,000 people, QOL score, schools, diversity

        Transportation

        Public transit, walking, biking, car commute, public transit commute, airport

        Geography

        Regional points, distance of Amazon, closest to Bezos home, #state fulfillment centers

        INSY 2299 · Session 7
        Metro Area Selection Example

        Our goal is to select the candidates for Amazon’s HQ2. How should we proceed?

        1. 1Explore/describe the different attributes/categories (Max, Min, Mean) by adding new rows below the given data set (rows 22–24)
        2. 2Think about the weight for each attribute (defaults added; they should add up to 1 (100%))
        3. 3Calculate a score for each metro area (and validate the score)
        4. 4Select the most appropriate metro area (“Winner!”) by using a function of your choice (e.g., IF function)
        5. 5Create a column that includes the rank of each city (1 should indicate the highest rank, for example by using the RANK function)
        6. 6Chart results (horizontal bar chart, optional)
